meta.descriptionEn: In 1964 a steel giant opened across the Narrows of New York, the longest suspension span in the world at 4,260 feet. Its two 693-foot towers are not parallel, because the curve of the Earth itself had to be calculated into the design. But the story is bigger than engineering. Decades of failed bridge and tunnel plans, a powerful planner named Robert Moses, and a fierce fight with Bay Ridge, where thousands of people lost their homes, shaped the bridge. Three workers fell to their deaths, a name was misspelled for nearly sixty years, and a toll rule caused congestion in Manhattan. Discover how the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge was dreamed, fought over and built.

articleEn: On the Narrows in New York stand two steel towers, each 693 feet tall and 4,260 feet apart. There is one odd thing about them: they are not parallel. At the top they are 1 5/8 inches farther apart than at the bottom. The reason is simple. The Earth is round. The towers are so far apart that engineers had to account for the curvature of the Earth.

This is the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge. When it opened on 21 November 1964, it had the longest suspension span in the world, meaning the longest central section. It carries 13 lanes, seven on the upper level and six on the lower. Today it is the only fixed crossing of the Narrows between Staten Island and Brooklyn.

But the story is about more than steel and mathematics. In Bay Ridge, 7,500 people had to leave their homes, and 3 workers died during construction. So where did the idea of joining Staten Island to Brooklyn come from, and why did the plan stall for decades? This article follows the story from the beginning: dreams, cancelled plans, political fights and the building of this steel giant.

articleEn: New York has five boroughs, but in the 1920s Staten Island was cut off from the rest of the city. Ferries were the only way to reach the other boroughs. The Staten Island Ferry ran to South Ferry in Manhattan, and other ferries ran to 39th Street and 69th Street in Brooklyn. There was no bridge.

In 1926 or 1927, structural engineer David B. Steinman proposed a new idea: why not build a bridge over the Narrows? The Narrows is the narrow waterway that connects New York Harbor to Lower New York Bay and the Atlantic Ocean. In other words, it is the sea gate of the city. Even today it is the only route for the large cruise ships and container ships that come into New York, which is why the height of the bridge mattered so much.

In 1928 the chambers of commerce of Brooklyn, Queens, Long Island and Staten Island announced that the Interboro Bridge Company had proposed a bridge. It was called the Liberty Bridge, and the proposal was sent to the United States Department of War. The estimated cost was 60 million dollars in 1928 money. In November 1929 engineers released plans for the 4,500-foot Liberty Bridge, whose towers were to be 800 feet tall. Supporters hoped it would bring growth to Staten Island. The Outerbridge Crossing and the Bayonne Bridge were also being built at the time. The bridge would have started in Bay Ridge, Brooklyn, and run to Staten Island, and there was a plan to connect it to a Crosstown Highway in Brooklyn.

But the plan never even came to a vote. The reason was Congressman Fiorello H. La Guardia, who blocked it. His position was simple: in his view, the public's needs should not be in the hands of private companies. So the Liberty Bridge stayed on paper. Residents of Bay Ridge were not in favor of any bridge either, because part of their neighborhood would have had to be demolished.

The man the bridge would eventually be named after was Giovanni da Verrazzano, who in 1524 became the first European explorer to enter New York Harbor. Did the dream of a bridge die with the Liberty Bridge? No. Plans for tunnels now came to the table.

articleEn: In 1923 an attempt began to connect Brooklyn and Staten Island. This was the Staten Island Tunnel, which would have carried the New York City Subway to Staten Island. Two years later, in 1925, the plan was cancelled. The idea of crossing the Narrows did not die, though, and new routes kept being considered. Engineers also proposed twin tunnels for cars, running from Fort Wadsworth on Staten Island to 97th Street in Brooklyn. In July 1929 the city set aside 5 million dollars for them, and the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad promised funding. Planning began that same month. The Brooklyn Chamber of Commerce was considering the bridge, the car tunnels and the subway tunnel all at once, but community groups could not agree.

Boring began in November 1930. The 11,000-foot twin tunnels were to be finished by 1937 and would have linked Hylan Boulevard to 86th Street. In January 1932 the work was halted indefinitely because of a lack of money, and nothing more came of it beyond a survey of the Brooklyn shoreline.

In February 1933 the U.S. House of Representatives approved a bill to build a suspension bridge over the Narrows. The project was expected to give jobs to 80,000 workers. Othmar H. Ammann, who was then involved with the Triborough Bridge, the Midtown Tunnel and the Golden Gate Bridge, showed interest in designing the new bridge. In December 1933 the city also approved a rapid transit tunnel under the Narrows. But in April 1934 the War Department openly opposed the bridge, believing that in wartime it could block the channel. The same argument had been used against the Brooklyn-Battery Bridge.

In 1936 Mayor La Guardia was given the authority to seek permission from Congress for a bridge. It would have cost 50 million dollars, but he preferred a tunnel. In 1943 the Board of Estimate set aside 50,000 dollars for a tunnel feasibility study, and now Bay Ridge turned against the tunnel too. In 1945 the Planning Commission put the cost of the tunnel at 73.5 million dollars, but La Guardia had turned against it. His words were: 'it is not my time'.
So would the Narrows stay without a bridge forever? No. As the tunnel idea ended, a powerful man took up the idea of a bridge.

articleEn: In September 1947 Robert Moses, chairman of the Triborough Bridge and Tunnel Authority, announced that the city would ask the War Department for permission to build a bridge over the Narrows. Moses had already studied the feasibility of a tunnel, and his conclusion was simple: a bridge would cost far less. Moses and Mayor William O'Dwyer both backed the plan, which was still being called the Liberty Bridge. The city filed its application in July 1948.

Donald Lawrence O'Toole, Bay Ridge's representative, strongly opposed the bridge. He feared it would spoil the character of the neighborhood, and he feared that in a war the bridge could block the Narrows. According to his poll, 33 people were opposed for every supporter. But in May 1949 the army approved the bridge despite Bay Ridge's fierce opposition, on the condition that construction begin within five years. By then a plan for a 6,540-foot span was ready. Financing of 78 million dollars remained, which was to come after the Battery Tunnel was completed in 1950. The early plans showed the bridge 237 feet above mean high water, enough for the 215-foot RMS Queen Mary to pass beneath.

Now the question was who would build it. Moses and Bayard F. Pope, acting chairman of the Port Authority, were both ready, provided the work was done efficiently. Public Works commissioner Frederick Zurmuhlen put the cost at 200 million dollars. He said construction should start soon to ease the rush on the East River bridges. Staten Islanders were cautious: the bridge connected them to the city, but it could cause traffic jams on the island. To Moses, it was necessary for the island's future.

Early in 1956 a transit study was carried out, but Moses rejected the idea of subway tracks on the bridge, saying it would be too expensive. In 1956 New Jersey's governor signed a bill allowing the Port Authority to build the bridge and lease it to the TBTA, which would buy it in 1967. According to Robert Caro, Moses deliberately left no room for mass transit on his bridges, so as to encourage private cars. The cost later rose to 320 million dollars. One big question remained: through which Brooklyn neighborhood would the bridge's approach pass?

articleEn: Where would the approach in Brooklyn run? The first plan was to link it to the Belt Parkway, but in 1957 Governor Harriman vetoed such a bill. Moses then made another proposal: extend the Gowanus Expressway along Seventh Avenue to the bridge. That meant a road through the middle of Bay Ridge. Bay Ridge residents wanted the approach to stay on the shoreline with the Belt Parkway. In their view the Seventh Avenue route would leave more than 1,500 families homeless.

In February 1958 the State Legislature passed a bill to take the approach along the Belt Parkway. But in August 1958 the city approved the Seventh Avenue route. In September 1958 Moses wrote to Mayor Wagner that further delay would cancel the bridge. The cost had reached 320 million dollars by then. In October 1958 the Board of Estimate approved the bridge plan, and proposals for a Narrows tunnel and for a bridge or tunnel from Brooklyn to Jersey City were rejected. The federal government required that the Seventh Avenue approach have 12 lanes, 6 on each level. It was already paying for the Clove Lakes and Gowanus Expressways. Finally, on 31 December 1958, after postponing the vote several times, the Board of Estimate approved the plans for the Seventh Avenue approach.

The decision deepened anger in Bay Ridge. The approach would leave 7,500 people homeless, while opponents had earlier spoken of more than 1,500 families. Staten Island reacted differently. More than twice as many people were being displaced there, but the island was getting better links to the rest of the city. The announcement was welcomed, real estate prices rose, and opposition was far smaller than in Bay Ridge.

Meanwhile David Steinman offered a rival proposal: build the bridge from Brooklyn straight to New Jersey rather than to Staten Island. Nelson Rockefeller, then a candidate for governor, initially supported it, but Moses persuaded him to back the Staten Island bridge. Governor Rockefeller then vetoed the Belt Parkway bill. In March 1959 the Board of Estimate decided to condemn land on Seventh Avenue. In April 1959 the bridge was named after Giovanni da Verrazzano, but the name was missing a z. That story comes later.

articleEn: Surveying on the bridge began in January 1959. Formal construction began on 14 August 1959 with a groundbreaking ceremony at the Staten Island anchorage. New Jersey governor Meyner, Mayor Wagner and Robert Moses were present. Rockefeller had been invited but did not come. In December 1959 the TBTA was given the funding and the responsibility for construction. The 4% interest limit on securities for the 320 million dollars was lifted until June 1965. Othmar Ammann became senior partner. Milton Brumer was chief engineer, Leopold Just was design engineer, and there were other engineers on the team, while John Murphy handled the construction of the span and cables.

The buildings on the anchorage sites were torn down first. Of Fort Hamilton's 138 acres, 36 were taken, and in return 12 million dollars of renovation was carried out. On the Brooklyn side, a 1,000-ton World War I monument stood in the way. It was placed on rolling logs and moved 370 feet. Each anchorage was 229 feet long and 129 feet wide, and the two together held 780,000 short tons of steel and concrete. Each had 66 openings for the cables.

Then two watertight caissons were sunk into the water, and the towers were to stand on them. The Staten Island caisson was 105 feet deep and took 47,000 cubic yards of concrete. The Brooklyn caisson was a much bigger job. It was 170 feet deep, took 83,000 cubic yards of concrete, and 145,000 cubic yards of muck had to be removed. Then came the 693-foot towers. Bethlehem Steel built the Staten Island tower and Harris Structural Company built the Brooklyn tower.

In March 1963 the American Bridge Company began spinning the cables. Each main cable is made of 26,108 wires, and the whole job involved 142,520 miles of wire. The process took six months, and the main cables were complete by August 1963. Suspender cables were then hung from them. The roadway deck sections were made in Jersey City, joined at the steelworks in Bayonne, and brought to the Narrows by barge. The first section was lifted in October 1963. Because the work went so fast, the TBTA decided to open the bridge in November 1964 instead of 1965, and the whole bridge was repainted in preparation.

For five years an average of 1,200 workers a day were employed, and about 10,000 people worked on it in total, not counting the approach workers. Writer Gay Talese recorded the construction in his 1964 book The Bridge, which includes drawings by Lili Rethi and photographs by Bruce Davidson. The bridge was nearly ready. But the Earth's curvature was hidden in its steel, and three lives were lost during construction. Their story comes in the next section.

articleEn: Now to the secret hidden in the bridge's steel. The two 693-foot towers stand 4,260 feet apart. Over such a distance the surface of the Earth does not stay flat but curves slightly. So engineers had to account for the curvature of the Earth in the design, and the result is that the two towers are not parallel. At the top they are 1 5/8 inches farther apart than at the bottom.

These towers do not use cross-bracing like ordinary suspension bridges. Instead, arched struts are fitted near the upper part of the towers and below the lower deck. Each tower contains about 1 million bolts and 3 million rivets. Together the two towers use 1,265,000 short tons of metal, more than three times the 365,000 short tons used in the Empire State Building. When the bridge was built, these towers were the tallest structures in the city outside Manhattan. Another surprise is linked to the weather. Steel cables expand in the heat, so in summer the upper roadway sits 12 feet lower than in winter.

But the cost of this enormous structure was not paid only in money. Three workers lost their lives during construction. The first was 58-year-old Paul Bassett, who fell from the deck in August 1962 and struck a tower. He was the first worker killed on the project. The second, Irving Rubin, also 58, fell from a bridge approach and died in July 1963. The third was 19-year-old Gerard McKee, who slipped from a catwalk and fell into the water in October 1963.

After his death the workers went on strike. In December 1963 there was a 5-day strike, and as a result temporary safety nets were hung under the deck. In the previous four years no nets had been provided. That leaves a bitter question: the nets went up only after three lives were lost, when the work was already four years old.

Then came opening day. Robert Moses did not invite any of the 12,000 workers to the ceremony. In protest the workers boycotted it and instead attended a Mass in memory of their three dead colleagues. The source mentions 12,000 workers, while elsewhere it says about 10,000 people in all worked on the construction. So what happened on the bridge on opening day, and how did the traffic surprise the planners?

articleEn: The bridge's upper deck opened on 21 November 1964. It cost $320 million, and a 50-cent toll was charged per car. The Staten Island approach had opened earlier, in January 1964. More than 5,000 people attended the opening ceremony, including 1,500 official guests. The governor, the mayor and the borough presidents of Brooklyn and Staten Island cut a golden ribbon and then set off across the bridge in a motorcade. From President Lyndon B. Johnson to Brooklyn Borough President Abe Stark, politicians at every level wrote speeches praising the bridge.

The bridge made an old route unnecessary. Five days after it opened, the ferry from Staten Island to Bay Ridge was shut down. In the first two months 1.86 million vehicles crossed, about 10% more than estimated, and the TBTA received about 1 million dollars in toll revenue. By the first anniversary 17 million motorists had crossed and $9 million in tolls had been collected. That was 34% more trips than the planners had predicted. Other roads felt the effect too. Average daily use of the Goethals Bridge rose 75%, while the Staten Island Ferry carried 5.5 million fewer passengers and 700,000 fewer vehicles.

The bridge was at first built with only one six-lane roadway. But Ammann had already installed extra trusses for a second roadway below. These trusses also stiffened the bridge, and after the 1940 collapse of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge, many bridges received similar design changes. In March 1969 the TBTA decided to build the lower deck for $22 million. It was not expected to be needed until 1978, but traffic had grown a great deal. The new six-lane deck opened on 28 June 1969. By comparison, the George Washington Bridge's lower deck was built 31 years after its 1931 opening.

This turned out to be Ammann's last bridge. He died in 1965, the year after it opened. It was also Moses's last big public works project in New York City. Moses believed the Verrazzano and Throgs Neck bridges would complete the city's expressway system, and that no more big bridges would be built for some time.

On 26 June 1976, for America's 200th anniversary, a 193 by 366 foot U.S. flag was hung on the bridge. It was called the largest flag in the world. But it tore apart three days later from rubbing against the suspender cables, when the wind was only 16 mph. In 1980 an even larger flag was hung on the steel grid. Ada Louise Huxtable asked whether $850,000 should be spent on upstaging the Statue of Liberty.

articleEn: Now the story of the name. During planning it was called the Narrows Bridge. In 1951 the Italian Historical Society proposed naming it after Verrazzano. Robert Moses first rejected the proposal. The Society's director, John N. LaCorte, persuaded several governors to declare April 17 Verrazzano Day. According to Gay Talese, a version of the name with a single z appeared in the construction contracts before 1959. In March 1960 Rockefeller made the name law.

In 1963, after President Kennedy's assassination, thousands signed a petition to name the bridge after him. But the name did not change. Robert F. Kennedy assured LaCorte that the bridge would keep its name. Instead, Idlewild Airport in Queens was named after Kennedy. At the opening many news outlets ignored the official name. According to the source, this was partly due to prejudice against Italian-Americans.

In 2016 Robert Nash, a student at St. Francis College, started a petition to spell Verrazzano correctly with two z's. Senators Golden and Lanza supported it. In 2017 the bill passed the Senate but failed in the Assembly in early 2018. In June 2018 the bill was approved, and on 1 October Cuomo signed it. The legal name thus became the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge. To save money the old signs were left as they were, and the first new sign went up in February 2020.

Before 1986 tolls were collected in both directions. After a bill by Guy V. Molinari, tolls were collected only from vehicles heading to Staten Island. In March 1986, under a pilot program, a $3.50 toll was charged instead of $1.75. The aim was to reduce traffic and pollution at the Staten Island toll booth. But the result was mixed. Revenue fell, and there was severe congestion on Canal Street in Lower Manhattan, because some drivers coming from New Jersey began using the Bayonne Bridge. Finally, in December 2019, President Trump signed the federal appropriations bill that ended the one-way toll mandate. On 1 December 2020 tolls returned in both directions.

A $1.5 billion renovation that began in 2011 had its first phase run until 2017. A seventh lane was added on the upper deck, and this HOV lane opened on 22 June 2017. In early 2025 the NTSB recommended a structural vulnerability assessment of the bridge after the collapse of Baltimore's Key Bridge. In June of the same year the MTA signaled a $249 million plan to replace the main cables and awarded the contract to Skanska Koch.

The bridge was built without a pedestrian walkway. It was considered expensive, and according to planners its absence helps prevent incidents of self-harm. A Life Is Worth Living sign and hotlines were placed at the approach in 2008, and a permanent barrier was installed between 2021 and 2022. If you are struggling, please do reach out for help.

Since 1976 the New York City Marathon has started from the Staten Island end of the bridge. The bridge is closed completely for the marathon and partially for the bike tour. Demands for a walkway or bike lane date back to opening day. The MTA put the cost of a multiple-use pathway at $400 million, and in March 2019 the project was shelved over safety concerns. Interestingly, another part of the source mentions a bicycle and pedestrian path in long-term plans. So the question is still open.

What can we learn from this bridge? Big projects are not only steel and cables. They also involve questions about local communities, decisions, safety and names. The 7,500 displaced people of Bay Ridge, the three workers and Ammann's last bridge are all part of this story. Would such projects be built differently today? What do you think? shorts.titleEn: The Bridge Towers That Aren't Parallel
shorts.text: کیا آپ جانتے ہیں کہ New York کے ایک پل کے دونوں towers آپس میں parallel نہیں ہیں؟ یہ Verrazzano–Narrows Bridge ہے۔ دونوں towers 693 feet اونچے ہیں اور 4,260 feet کے فاصلے پر کھڑے ہیں۔ اتنے فاصلے پر زمین ہلکی سی گول ہوتی ہے۔ اس لیے engineers کو Earth کی curvature کا حساب لگانا پڑا۔ نتیجہ یہ کہ towers اوپر سے نیچے کے مقابلے میں 1 اور 5/8 inch زیادہ دور ہیں۔ یہ پل 21 November 1964 کو کھلا، تو دنیا کا سب سے لمبا suspension span تھا۔ آج بھی یہ Staten Island اور Brooklyn کے درمیان Narrows کا واحد fixed crossing ہے۔ مگر اس پل کا خیال سب سے پہلے کس نے پیش کیا تھا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Kya aap jante hain ke New York ke aik pul ke dono towers aapas mein parallel nahin hain? Yeh Verrazzano–Narrows Bridge hai. Dono towers 693 feet unchay hain aur 4,260 feet ke fasle par khare hain. Itne fasle par zameen halki si gol hoti hai. Is liye engineers ko Earth ki curvature ka hisab lagana para. Nateeja yeh ke towers upar se neeche ke muqable mein 1 aur 5/8 inch zyada door hain. Yeh pul 21 November 1964 ko khula, to duniya ka sab se lamba suspension span tha. Aaj bhi yeh Staten Island aur Brooklyn ke darmiyan Narrows ka wahid fixed crossing hai. Magar is pul ka khayal sab se pehle kis ne pesh kiya tha? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
The Verrazzano–Narrows Bridge towers are 1 5/8 inches farther apart at the top because of Earth's curvature.
A quick look at one of the strangest design facts of a famous New York bridge.

shorts.titleEn: The Road That Almost Cancelled a Giant Bridge
shorts.hook: Ek Rasta, Poora Pul Khatre Mein
shorts.text: کیا ایک سڑک کا راستہ پورے پل کو روک سکتا تھا؟ یہ Brooklyn کے Bay Ridge میں ہوا۔ Robert Moses نے تجویز دی کہ Gowanus Expressway کو Seventh Avenue کے راستے پل تک لایا جائے۔ یعنی Bay Ridge کے بیچ سے۔ رہنے والے چاہتے تھے کہ approach Belt Parkway کے ساتھ ساحل پر رہے۔ ان کے مطابق Seventh Avenue والا راستہ 1,500 سے زیادہ خاندانوں کو بے گھر کرتا۔ August 1958 میں شہر نے Seventh Avenue کا راستہ منظور کر دیا۔ پھر Moses نے mayor Wagner کو لکھا کہ مزید تاخیر ہوئی تو پل cancel ہو جائے گا۔ 31 December 1958 کو Board of Estimate نے آخرکار منظوری دے دی۔ مگر اس فیصلے سے کتنے لوگ متاثر ہوئے؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Kya aik sarak ka rasta poore pul ko rok sakta tha? Yeh Brooklyn ke Bay Ridge mein hua. Robert Moses ne tajweez di ke Gowanus Expressway ko Seventh Avenue ke raste pul tak laya jaye. Yani Bay Ridge ke beech se. Rehne walay chahtay thay ke approach Belt Parkway ke sath sahil par rahe. Un ke mutabiq Seventh Avenue wala rasta 1,500 se zyada khandanon ko be ghar karta. August 1958 mein shehar ne Seventh Avenue ka rasta manzoor kar diya. Phir Moses ne mayor Wagner ko likha ke mazeed takheer hui to pul cancel ho jaye ga. 31 December 1958 ko Board of Estimate ne akhirkar manzoori de di. Magar is faisle se kitne log mutasir hue? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
The fight over the Brooklyn approach in Bay Ridge nearly derailed the Verrazzano–Narrows Bridge in 1958.
Robert Moses, local residents and the Board of Estimate clashed over Seventh Avenue.
